title: Sputnik 1
subtitle: Soviet Union · First artificial satellite, 1957–1958

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: Soviet Union (design team led by Sergei Korolev)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 4 October 1957, from the site now called Baikonur Cosmodrome

essay:
Sputnik 1 was the first artificial satellite. The Soviet Union launched it on 4 October 1957 from the site in Kazakhstan now known as the Baikonur Cosmodrome, as a contribution to the International Geophysical Year. The rocket was an R-7, built as an intercontinental ballistic missile. Sergei Korolev had planned a larger scientific satellite, but when that project fell behind he had a much simpler one designed and built quickly.

The satellite was a pressurized aluminium-alloy sphere weighing 184 lb (about 83 kg). It carried no scientific instruments, only a radio transmitter whose beeping signal amateur operators around the world could pick up. Even so, tracking it was useful: how long it stayed in orbit gave information on the density of the upper atmosphere, and its signals tested radio propagation and tracking methods. It went around Earth about every 90 minutes. The rocket's large core stage also reached orbit, and because it was more reflective, most observers who saw something in the sky were watching the rocket rather than the satellite.

The batteries ran out on 26 October 1957 and Sputnik re-entered the atmosphere on 4 January 1958. Its launch prompted congressional hearings in the United States that led to the creation of NASA in 1958.

image.caption: Full-scale mockup of Sputnik 1 on display at the Paris Air Show in 1975.

sources.title: NASA: 65 Years Ago, Sputnik Ushers in the Space Age

title: Explorer 1
subtitle: United States · First US satellite, 1958

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: US Army Ballistic Missile Agency with JPL

facts.label: Key result
facts.value: Detected the radiation belts now named after James Van Allen

essay:
Explorer 1 was the first satellite launched by the United States. It went up from Cape Canaveral on a Jupiter-C rocket at 10:48 p.m. EST on 31 January 1958, a little under four months after Sputnik 1. The rocket came from the Army Ballistic Missile Agency in Huntsville under Wernher von Braun: a modified Redstone missile topped with upper stages of clustered solid-propellant motors built by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. The urgency came partly from the failure of the Navy's Vanguard rocket, which exploded on the pad in December 1957.

The science payload was designed by James Van Allen of the University of Iowa. It included a cosmic-ray detector, temperature sensors, a micrometeorite microphone and erosion gauges, and two transmitters. The cosmic-ray detector returned counts that pointed to belts of charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field, now called the Van Allen radiation belts.

Once orbit was confirmed, Pickering, Van Allen and von Braun announced the success at a press conference in Washington in the early hours of 1 February. The satellite's last transmission came on 23 May 1958.

image.caption: Explorer 1, the first US satellite.

title: Vostok 1
subtitle: Soviet Union · First human spaceflight, 1961

facts.label: Landing
facts.value: Saratov region, about 26 km south-west of Engels

essay:
Vostok 1 carried the first person into space. Cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin of the Soviet Union lifted off at 9:07 a.m. Moscow time on 12 April 1961, made a single orbit of Earth and was back on the ground 108 minutes later. In orbit the spacecraft travelled at about 27,400 km/h.

The flight was largely automated. Re-entry was controlled by a computer on board rather than flown by hand. The landing also differed from the early American human spaceflight programme. Instead of riding the capsule all the way down, Gagarin ejected from the spacecraft during the descent and landed separately under his own parachute, in the Saratov region of the Soviet Union about 26 km south-west of the town of Engels.

The mission came three and a half years after Sputnik 1 and showed that a person could be launched into orbit, survive weightlessness and the heat of re-entry, and be recovered safely. Every later crewed programme, from Mercury and Apollo to the International Space Station, built on that first single orbit.

sources.title: NASA: April 1961 – First Human Entered Space
NASA StarChild: The launch of Vostok 1

title: Mariner 2
subtitle: NASA · Venus flyby, 1962

facts.label: Last contact
facts.value: 3 January 1963, at 86.7 million km from Earth

essay:
Mariner 2 was the first successful planetary mission: the first spacecraft to return data from a close pass of another planet. It was launched on 27 August 1962, 36 days after its twin Mariner 1 was lost shortly after launch, and carried the same set of instruments.

The spacecraft had no camera. Its main instruments were microwave and infrared radiometers, a magnetometer, a cosmic dust detector, a solar plasma spectrometer and energetic particle detectors. After a course correction on 4 September, it passed Venus on 14 December 1962 at a range of 34,854 km. During a 42-minute scan the radiometers swept across the night side, the terminator and the day side of the planet.

The readings showed little difference in temperature between the day and night sides, and the microwave radiometer indicated values well above 200 °C, far hotter than many scientists had expected. Mariner 2 also found a dense cloud layer roughly 56 to 80 km above the surface and detected no planetary magnetic field, though it may simply have been too far away to see one. It also made measurements of the interplanetary medium during the cruise to Venus and after the flyby. NASA kept in contact until 3 January 1963, when the probe was 86.7 million km from Earth, then a record distance for a deep space probe.

image.caption: Artist's concept of Mariner 2, the first spacecraft to fly past Venus.

title: Mariner 4
subtitle: NASA · Mars flyby, 1964–1967

facts.label: Images returned
facts.value: 21 full images plus 22 lines of a 22nd

essay:
Mariner 4 made the first successful flyby of Mars and returned the first close-up pictures of another planet. Its twin, Mariner 3, launched three weeks earlier but its payload shroud failed to separate, leaving it inert in solar orbit. Mariner 4 flew with a redesigned all-metal shroud and had no such problem.

After a single course correction in December 1964, the spacecraft passed Mars on the evening of 14 July 1965 US time at a range of 9,846 km. About 40 minutes before closest approach its TV camera began taking 21 images, plus 22 lines of a 22nd, through red and green filters. The pictures showed an old, heavily cratered surface more like the Moon than the Earth. Before the computers had finished processing the first frame, team members printed the raw numbers on strips of paper and coloured them in by hand.

After the flyby Mariner 4 passed behind Mars as seen from Earth, so its radio signal travelled through the Martian atmosphere. The result showed a very low surface pressure, which meant future landers would need rockets as well as parachutes. The probe also measured daytime surface temperatures of about −100 °C. Contact continued intermittently until 31 December 1967.

image.caption: Mariner 4 image of the 151 km Mars crater later named Mariner after the spacecraft.

title: Luna 9
subtitle: Soviet Union · Moon lander, 1966

facts.label: Key result
facts.value: First survivable landing on the Moon and first photographs from its surface

essay:
Luna 9 was the first spacecraft to land on the Moon without being destroyed and the first to send back pictures from the lunar surface. It was launched by the Soviet Union on 31 January 1966 and touched down on 3 February 1966 at 18:44:52 UTC in Oceanus Procellarum, the Ocean of Storms, at 7.08° N, 295.63° E.

Earlier Soviet attempts had shown how hard this was. Luna 5, 7 and 8, launched in 1965, all hit the Moon instead of landing softly, and Luna 6 missed it entirely. Luna 9 succeeded where they had failed. Once on the surface, its small lander transmitted close-up photographs of the ground around it. Together with later landers such as Luna 13, the purpose of these images was to study the lunar surface at close range and help judge whether crewed landings would be feasible.

NSSDCA holds photographic data from Luna 9 along with images from Luna 3, 13, 21 and 22 and several Zond flights. Luna 9 belongs to a Soviet lunar programme that achieved several firsts, including the first impact on the Moon, the first images of the far side, the first soft landing and the first lunar orbiter.

image.caption: Close-up of the surface of Oceanus Procellarum taken by the Luna 9 lander in February 1966.

sources.title: NSSDCA: Soviet Missions to the Moon
NASA Science: First Photo from the Surface of the Moon

title: Apollo 8
subtitle: NASA · First crewed lunar orbit, 1968
essay:
Apollo 8 was the first crewed spacecraft to leave Earth orbit and reach the Moon, and the first crewed launch of the Saturn V rocket. Frank Borman, James Lovell and William Anders lifted off on 21 December 1968 and entered lunar orbit on 24 December.

The flight tested the Apollo command and service module, with its communications, tracking and life-support systems, in deep space and in lunar orbit. No lunar module flew on this mission; a test article of the same mass was carried in its place as ballast. After a first elliptical orbit the spacecraft settled into a near-circular orbit about 110 km above the surface and completed 10 orbits in all. The crew photographed both the near side and the far side to map landmarks and terrain for later landing missions, and made six live television broadcasts, including a reading from the book of Genesis on Christmas Eve.

On 24 December Anders photographed Earth rising over the lunar horizon. The picture is known as Earthrise. The engine burn to leave lunar orbit came on 25 December, and the command module splashed down in the Pacific on 27 December 1968 after a flight of just over six days. The command module is now on display at the Museum of Science and Industry in Chicago.

image.caption: Earthrise: Earth above the lunar horizon, photographed from Apollo 8 on 24 December 1968.

title: Apollo 11
subtitle: NASA · First crewed Moon landing, 1969

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 16 July 1969, 13:32 UTC, Kennedy Space Center pad 39A

facts.label: Samples returned
facts.value: 21.55 kg of lunar rock and soil

essay:
Apollo 11 was the first mission to land people on the Moon and return them to Earth. Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins launched on a Saturn V from Kennedy Space Center on 16 July 1969 and entered lunar orbit on 19 July.

On 20 July Armstrong and Aldrin separated in the lunar module Eagle while Collins stayed in orbit in the command module. Eagle landed in Mare Tranquillitatis, the Sea of Tranquility, at 20:17:40 UTC. Armstrong stepped onto the surface at 02:56 UTC on 21 July and Aldrin followed 19 minutes later. During a single moonwalk lasting a little over two hours they set up a package of scientific experiments, took photographs and collected 21.55 kg of rock and soil, covering about 250 m in total.

Eagle's ascent stage lifted off on 21 July after 21 hours 36 minutes on the surface and docked with the command module in lunar orbit. The crew left the Moon on 22 July and splashed down in the Pacific on 24 July, about 24 km from the recovery ship USS Hornet, after a flight of 195 hours 18 minutes. NASA described the spacecraft's performance as excellent throughout the mission.

image.caption: The Apollo 11 lunar module ascent stage returning from the surface, with Earth in the background, photographed from the command module.

sources.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: Apollo 11 Command and Service Module

title: Venera 7
subtitle: Soviet Union · Venus lander, 1970

facts.label: Key result
facts.value: First successful soft landing of a spacecraft on another planet

essay:
Venera 7 was the first spacecraft to make a soft landing on another planet and send back data from its surface. The Soviet Union launched it toward Venus on 17 August 1970, and it reached the planet later the same year.

It followed a series of Soviet atmospheric probes. Venera 4 in 1967 was the first to return data on the composition of the Venusian atmosphere, and Veneras 5 and 6 in 1969 detected nitrogen and oxygen, but all three were crushed by the pressure before they reached the ground. Venera 7 was designed as a lander, and its capsule reached the surface.

From the ground it measured the surface temperature and pressure of Venus, the first such measurements made on the surface of another planet. A companion attempt launched five days after Venera 7, Cosmos 359, failed. Later Soviet landers built on its design: Venera 8 measured wind speed during its descent in 1972, and Veneras 9 and 10 in 1975 combined landers with orbiters.

image.caption: Global view of Venus built from Magellan radar, Pioneer Venus and Venera data.

title: Pioneer 10
subtitle: NASA · Jupiter flyby, 1972–2003

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (mission managed by Ames Research Center)

essay:
Pioneer 10 was NASA's first mission to the outer planets and the first spacecraft to fly past Jupiter. It was also the first to travel through the main asteroid belt, the first to fly beyond the orbit of Mars and the first to run entirely on nuclear electrical power, from two radioisotope thermoelectric generators.

Launched in March 1972, it left Earth faster than any previous human-made object. It entered the asteroid belt in July 1972 and emerged in February 1973, having met fewer dust impacts than expected. Closest approach to Jupiter came on 4 December 1973 at 130,354 km, at about 126,000 km/h. By then it was returning better pictures of the planet than any Earth-based telescope could take. Like Pioneer 11, it carries a metal plaque showing where and when it was built.

Jupiter's gravity put Pioneer 10 on a path out of the solar system. It crossed the orbit of Neptune on 13 June 1983. Routine tracking ended on 31 March 1997 for budget reasons, though occasional contact continued. The last signal arrived on 23 January 2003 from 12.23 billion km away, and a final attempt in February 2003 detected nothing. The spacecraft is heading in the general direction of the red star Aldebaran in Taurus, about 68 light years away.

image.caption: Jupiter photographed by Pioneer 10 from 2,584,000 km in December 1973, with a moon at upper right.

title: Pioneer 11
subtitle: NASA · Jupiter and Saturn flyby, 1973–1995

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (mission managed by Ames Research Center)

facts.label: Jupiter flyby
facts.value: 3 December 1974 at about 42,500 km from the cloud tops

essay:
Pioneer 11 was the second spacecraft to visit Jupiter and the first to fly past Saturn. It was launched in April 1973, about a year after its twin, Pioneer 10.

Mid-course corrections sent it much closer to Jupiter than Pioneer 10 and over the planet's polar regions. On 3 December 1974 it passed about 42,500 km above the cloud tops at more than 171,000 km/h, then the fastest speed of any human-made object. Because it crossed the radiation belts so quickly, it spent less time in them than its twin despite flying closer. It returned the first pictures of Jupiter's polar regions, better views of the Great Red Spot and about 200 images of Jupiter's moons.

Jupiter's gravity then swung Pioneer 11 back across the solar system toward Saturn. It detected Saturn's bow shock on 31 August 1979, about 1.5 million km from the planet, which was the first firm evidence that Saturn has a magnetic field. Closest approach came on 1 September 1979, when its path through the outer ring region took it within about 21,000 km of Saturn. The spacecraft crossed the orbit of Neptune in 1990. NASA Ames made last contact on 30 September 1995, and the last engineering data arrived on 24 November 1995. Pioneer 11 is on a course out of the solar system.

image.caption: Atlas-Centaur rocket launching Pioneer 11 (then called Pioneer G) from Cape Canaveral in April 1973.

title: Mariner 10
subtitle: NASA · Venus and Mercury flybys, 1973–1975
essay:
Mariner 10 was the first spacecraft sent to Mercury and the first to explore two planets on one mission. It was also the first to use the gravity of one planet to reach another: a close pass of Venus on 5 February 1974 bent its path toward Mercury. During that flyby it returned 4,165 photographs of Venus.

Mariner 10 flew past Mercury three times. The first encounter, on 29 March 1974 at 703 km, showed a heavily cratered, Moon-like surface with ridges and chaotic terrain. The magnetometers found a weak magnetic field, and an occultation experiment showed no significant atmosphere. After looping around the Sun, and with further course corrections, it returned to the planet on 21 September 1974 and again on 16 March 1975, the last pass at only 327 km. Between encounters the team used the pressure of sunlight on the solar panels and high-gain antenna to control the spacecraft's orientation, the first time a probe had relied on this as a major means of attitude control.

Across the three flybys Mariner 10 took more than 2,700 pictures covering nearly half of Mercury's surface, with detail down to about 100 m. The most striking feature was the Caloris basin, a ringed impact structure about 2,500 km across. Contact ended on 24 March 1975 when the attitude-control gas ran out. No other spacecraft visited Mercury for more than 30 years.

image.caption: Venus photographed by Mariner 10 as it sped away from the planet in February 1974, reprocessed in 2020.

title: Viking 1
subtitle: NASA · Mars orbiter and lander, 1975–1982
essay:
Viking 1 made the first fully successful landing on Mars and returned the first images from its surface. The Soviet Mars 3 lander had reached the surface in 1971, but contact was lost seconds after touchdown.

The spacecraft had two parts: an orbiter derived from the Mariner design and a lander that resembled a much larger version of the Surveyor lunar lander, powered by two radioisotope generators. It entered Mars orbit on 19 June 1976. Orbiter photographs showed that the planned landing site in the Chryse region was rougher than expected, so the team chose a new site on the western slopes of Chryse Planitia. The lander touched down there on 20 July 1976 and took its first picture of rocks and soil minutes later.

The lander carried cameras, a weather station, a seismometer, an X-ray fluorescence spectrometer, a gas chromatograph-mass spectrometer and a biology laboratory designed to look for signs of life in the soil. With its twin Viking 2, the mission's two orbiters returned 52,663 images and mapped about 97 percent of Mars at around 300 m resolution, while the two landers sent back 4,500 photographs. The Viking 1 orbiter was shut down on 7 August 1980 after running out of attitude-control propellant. The lander kept working until 11 November 1982, when a faulty command ended contact.

image.caption: The first photograph taken on the surface of Mars, by the Viking 1 lander minutes after touchdown on 20 July 1976.

title: Voyager 1
subtitle: NASA · Jupiter, Saturn and interstellar space, 1977–present
essay:
Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object. It was launched on 5 September 1977, about two weeks after its twin Voyager 2, but took a faster route and overtook it on 15 December 1977.

At Jupiter, which it passed on 5 March 1979, Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around the planet and two new moons, Thebe and Metis. At Saturn, on 12 November 1980, it found five new moons and a new ring, the G ring. The Saturn encounter included a close pass of Titan, and the trajectory chosen for it sent the spacecraft up and out of the plane of the planets, ending its planetary tour.

On 17 February 1998 it passed Pioneer 10 to become the most distant spacecraft, and in August 2012 it crossed the heliopause into interstellar space, the first spacecraft to do so. Its radioisotope generators lose power every year, so the team has been switching instruments off in a planned order. The latest, the low-energy charged particle instrument on 17 April 2026, left the magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem running. On 18 November 2026 Voyager 1 is due to be 25.902 billion km from Earth, the distance light travels in one day.

image.caption: Jupiter with its moons Io (left) and Europa, photographed by Voyager 1 on 13 February 1979.

sources.title: NASA Science: Where Are Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 Now?

title: Voyager 2
subtitle: NASA · Tour of the four giant planets, 1977–present

facts.label: Instruments operating (October 2026)
facts.value: Cosmic ray subsystem, magnetometer, plasma wave subsystem

essay:
Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to have visited all four giant planets and the only one to have flown past Uranus and Neptune. It was launched on 20 August 1977, two weeks before Voyager 1.

The two Voyagers replaced a cancelled plan for a 'Grand Tour' of the outer planets. They were designed for Jupiter and Saturn, but in 1974 mission planners proposed that if the first spacecraft succeeded, the second could be sent on to Uranus and Neptune using gravity assists. Voyager 2 passed Jupiter on 9 July 1979, where it found a 14th moon, and Saturn on 25 August 1981. It reached Uranus on 24 January 1986, discovering 10 new moons and two new rings. At Neptune on 25 August 1989 it found five moons, four rings and a large storm called the Great Dark Spot. These remain the only close-up observations of either ice giant.

Voyager 2 crossed the solar wind's termination shock on 30 August 2007 and entered interstellar space in 2018, becoming the second spacecraft to do so. Like its twin it carries the Golden Record of sounds and images from Earth. To save power, the team turned off its plasma science instrument in September 2024 and its low-energy charged particle instrument in March 2025. As of October 2026 the cosmic ray subsystem, magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem are still on.

image.caption: Neptune and its Great Dark Spot, from Voyager 2 images taken four days before closest approach in August 1989.

sources.title: NASA Science: Where Are Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 Now?

title: Hubble Space Telescope
subtitle: NASA · Space telescope in Earth orbit, 1990–present
essay:
The Hubble Space Telescope is a 2.4 m reflecting telescope in low Earth orbit, about 483 km up. It was carried into space and released by the space shuttle Discovery in April 1990. It is about the size of a large school bus and weighs about 12,200 kg.

Its first images were blurred. The edge of the primary mirror had been ground too flat by a fraction of the width of a human hair, because of a flaw in the test equipment used to check its shape. The first servicing mission in December 1993 installed a new camera with built-in corrective optics and a set of small mirrors to correct the other instruments. Four more servicing missions followed, the last in May 2009, replacing instruments and worn parts and extending the telescope's life.

Hubble has made more than 1.7 million observations, and more than 23,000 peer-reviewed papers have been published from its data. Its work ranges from measuring the composition of exoplanet atmospheres to the discovery of dark energy. It has observed galaxies more than 13.4 billion light-years away. It remains in operation, and engineers have used other sensors on the spacecraft to make up for gyroscopes that have failed.

image.caption: The Hubble Space Telescope over Earth after release from Space Shuttle Discovery in February 1997.

sources.title: NASA Science: Hubble by the Numbers
NASA Science: The History of Hubble

title: Galileo
subtitle: NASA · Jupiter orbiter and probe, 1989–2003

facts.label: Launch vehicle
facts.value: Space Shuttle Atlantis (STS-34) with Inertial Upper Stage

essay:
Galileo was the first spacecraft to orbit an outer planet and the first to drop a probe into a giant planet's atmosphere. It was launched from the space shuttle Atlantis on 18 October 1989 and reached Jupiter by a roundabout route that used one flyby of Venus and two of Earth.

On the way it made the first flyby of an asteroid, Gaspra, in 1991, followed by Ida in 1993, and in July 1994 it made the first, and so far only, direct observation of a comet hitting a planet, as fragments of Shoemaker-Levy 9 struck Jupiter. On 7 December 1995 it entered orbit, and its probe, released five months earlier, descended into the atmosphere at 47.6 km/s. The probe found that the relative abundances of elements in Jupiter's atmosphere differ from the Sun's.

Over almost eight years the orbiter circled Jupiter 34 times and made 35 close flybys of its moons. It found that Io's volcanism may be about 100 times more active than Earth's and that Ganymede has its own magnetic field, the first moon known to have one. Its magnetic measurements pointed to salty liquid water beneath the surfaces of Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. To keep the spacecraft from ever contaminating a possible ocean on Europa, NASA sent it into Jupiter's atmosphere on 21 September 2003.

image.caption: Artist's rendering of the Galileo spacecraft passing Jupiter's volcanic moon Io.

title: Ulysses
subtitle: ESA and NASA · Solar polar orbiter, 1990–2009

facts.label: Launch vehicle
facts.value: Space Shuttle Discovery (STS-41) with IUS and PAM-S upper stages

essay:
Ulysses was the first mission to study the space environment above and below the poles of the Sun. ESA built the spacecraft and NASA provided its radioisotope power source, the shuttle launch and tracking through the Deep Space Network; the instruments came from both sides.

Leaving the plane of the planets takes a great deal of energy, so Ulysses first flew to Jupiter. After launch from the space shuttle Discovery in October 1990 it left Earth at about 15.4 km/s, then the fastest velocity achieved by a human-made object. Jupiter's gravity on 8 February 1992 bent its path steeply out of the ecliptic into an orbit that carried it over the Sun's south pole in 1994 and north pole in 1995, reaching 80.2° solar latitude.

Ulysses found that the solar wind blows faster over the poles than near the equator, and that the magnetic field at the Sun's poles is much weaker than had been assumed. It tracked the solar wind weakening to a 50-year low in 2008. By chance it flew through the tails of three comets, showing that comet tails can be much longer than expected. The mission completed nearly three orbits of the Sun over 18 years, more than four times its design life, and contact ended on 30 June 2009.

image.caption: Ulysses and its upper stages moving away from Space Shuttle Discovery after release on 6 October 1990.

title: SOHO
subtitle: ESA and NASA · Solar observatory at L1, 1995–present

facts.label: Orbit
facts.value: Halo orbit around the Sun–Earth L1 point, 1.5 million km from Earth

essay:
The Solar and Heliospheric Observatory, SOHO, is a joint ESA and NASA mission that has watched the Sun continuously since the 1990s. ESA leads the mission; NASA supplied three of its twelve instruments, the launch and flight operations support. SOHO sits about 1.5 million km from Earth, orbiting the Sun–Earth L1 point, where it has an uninterrupted view of the Sun.

SOHO's instruments study the Sun from its core to its outer atmosphere. Helioseismology measurements probe the interior, ultraviolet telescopes image the hot corona, and the LASCO coronagraphs block the bright disc to show the outer corona and the coronal mass ejections that drive space weather at Earth. Among its findings is the origin of the fast solar wind at the edges of large magnetic cells near the Sun's poles.

Its planned mission ended in 1998. In June of that year contact was lost for four months and the spacecraft was found spinning and short of power, but controllers recovered it, and after its gyroscopes failed ESA developed a way to point it using reaction wheels alone. Extended many times since, SOHO has now observed two full 11-year solar cycles and most of a third, and marked 30 years of operation in December 2025. Through LASCO, more than 70 people from 18 countries have used its images to find more than 5,000 comets, more than half of all comets known.

image.caption: Atlas IIAS rocket launching SOHO from Cape Canaveral on 2 December 1995.

title: Mars Pathfinder
subtitle: NASA · Mars lander and rover, 1996–1997

facts.label: Images returned
facts.value: More than 16,500 from the lander and 550 from the rover

essay:
Mars Pathfinder delivered the first robotic rover to Mars. It began as a technology demonstration, testing a cheaper way to land on the planet and to explore it with a small free-roaming vehicle.

Pathfinder entered the atmosphere directly from its approach path rather than going into orbit first. A parachute slowed its descent through the thin atmosphere, and a cluster of large airbags inflated around the lander to cushion the impact. It hit the ground on 4 July 1997 at about 14 m/s and bounced about 15 times, as high as 15 m, before rolling to a stop roughly 1 km from where it first struck. It was the first time this airbag technique had been used.

The landing site was Ares Vallis. The 10.6 kg rover Sojourner rolled off the lander on a pair of deployable ramps and studied the rocks and soil nearby, while the lander analysed the atmosphere and weather. By the final transmission on 27 September 1997 the mission had returned more than 16,500 images from the lander, 550 from the rover, more than 15 chemical analyses of rocks and soil, and extensive weather data. Its findings suggested that Mars was once warm and wet.

image.caption: The Sojourner rover, still latched to the Mars Pathfinder lander, on the first day after landing.

title: Cassini–Huygens
subtitle: NASA, ESA and ASI · Saturn orbiter and Titan probe, 1997–2017

facts.label: Agencies
facts.value: NASA, ESA and the Italian Space Agency (ASI)

essay:
Cassini–Huygens was the first mission to orbit Saturn. NASA built the Cassini orbiter, ESA supplied the Huygens probe for Titan, and the Italian Space Agency contributed hardware. The spacecraft launched on a Titan IVB/Centaur on 15 October 1997 and reached Saturn on 1 July 2004 after gravity assists from Venus twice, Earth and Jupiter.

Huygens separated on 24 December 2004 and descended through Titan's thick atmosphere on 14 January 2005. Over 13 years Cassini completed 294 orbits of Saturn, made 127 targeted flybys of Titan and 23 of Enceladus, and took 453,048 images. On Titan it found three seas and hundreds of small lakes, with methane rivers running into a methane sea. At Enceladus it found jets of ice and water vapour spraying from fractures near the south pole, fed by an ocean beneath the ice. The mission counts oceans at both Titan and Enceladus among its discoveries, along with six named moons.

Having used almost all of its propellant, Cassini ended its mission with a phase called the Grand Finale. On 15 September 2017 it was steered into Saturn's atmosphere so that it could never crash into, and contaminate, Enceladus or Titan. Lessons from its orbital tour were used to plan NASA's Europa Clipper mission.

image.caption: Saturn, its rings and, far in the background, Earth, imaged by Cassini from Saturn's shadow on 19 July 2013.

title: International Space Station
subtitle: NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA and CSA · Crewed station in Earth orbit, 1998–present

facts.label: Partner agencies
facts.value: NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA, CSA (15 countries)

facts.label: Orbit
facts.value: About 400 km (250 miles) up, at about 28,000 km/h (17,500 mph)

essay:
The International Space Station is a crewed laboratory in low Earth orbit, built and operated by five space agencies from 15 countries: NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA and the Canadian Space Agency. The first module, the Russian-launched Zarya, went up on a Proton-K rocket on 20 November 1998. The station has been continuously occupied since November 2000, and on 2 November 2025 it marked 25 years of uninterrupted human presence.

Its large modules and other parts were delivered on 42 assembly flights, 37 of them by the US space shuttle and five by Russian Proton and Soyuz rockets. The finished structure is 109 m from end to end, close to the length of an American football field including the end zones, and its solar arrays span the same distance. It orbits about 400 km above Earth at roughly 28,000 km/h, circling the planet about every 90 minutes, or 16 times a day.

A typical crew is seven people. Cargo arrives on several vehicles, including Northrop Grumman's Cygnus, SpaceX's Dragon and Russia's Progress, and up to eight spacecraft can be docked at once. Thousands of experiments have been carried out on board, leading to advances in medicine, materials science and climate research, and crews exercise at least two hours a day to limit the loss of muscle and bone in weightlessness. The station's path takes it over about 90 percent of the world's population, and NASA's Spot the Station app gives alerts for visible passes.

image.caption: The International Space Station photographed from a departing Soyuz spacecraft on 4 October 2018.

sources.title: NASA: Space Station Facts and Figures

title: Spirit and Opportunity
subtitle: NASA · Mars Exploration Rovers, 2003–2019

facts.label: Spirit launch
facts.value: 10 June 2003, 17:58 UTC, Delta II, Cape Canaveral

essay:
Spirit and Opportunity were twin rovers, each about the size of a golf cart and weighing 185 kg. They were sent to opposite sides of Mars to sites thought to have been affected by liquid water, with the job of examining rocks and soil for clues to the planet's watery past. Both landed inside protective airbags in January 2004, and both worked far longer than planned: Spirit about 25 times its intended lifetime and Opportunity about 60 times.

Spirit landed in Gusev crater and spent much of its mission in the Columbia Hills. In 2007, while dragging a jammed front wheel, it scraped up a patch of nearly pure silica, strong evidence that hot springs or steam vents had once existed there. In May 2009 it became stuck in soft soil near a plateau called Home Plate. It sent its last signal in March 2010, and NASA ended efforts to contact it on 25 May 2011, after six years, two months and 19 days of work.

Opportunity landed in Meridiani Planum and found evidence that Mars may once have been able to support microbial life. It later drove to the 22 km Endeavour crater, arriving in August 2011, and became the first vehicle to cover a marathon distance on another world. A planet-wide dust storm cut off communication in June 2018, and NASA declared the mission over on 13 February 2019. Its distance record of 45.16 km stood until Perseverance passed it in October 2026.

image.caption: Self-portrait of Opportunity in Perseverance Valley on Endeavour crater, taken with its Microscopic Imager for its 5,000th Martian day.

title: MESSENGER
subtitle: NASA · Mercury orbiter, 2004–2015

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (mission managed by Johns Hopkins APL)

facts.label: Flybys en route
facts.value: Earth once, Venus twice, Mercury three times

essay:
MESSENGER (MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging) was the first spacecraft to orbit Mercury and the first mission to the planet since Mariner 10 three decades earlier. It was the seventh mission in NASA's Discovery programme.

Reaching Mercury means losing a great deal of speed, since anything falling toward the Sun accelerates. MESSENGER did this with six gravity-assist flybys over six and a half years: one of Earth, two of Venus and three of Mercury itself. It finally entered orbit on 18 March 2011 and began formal science operations in April.

During more than four years in orbit it mapped the whole planet in monochrome and in colour, took more than 200,000 images, and measured Mercury's surface composition and its internal magnetic field, which turned out to be offset well to the north of the planet's centre. It found evidence of past volcanic activity and large amounts of water in Mercury's thin exosphere. It also confirmed that deposits in permanently shadowed craters near the poles are mostly water ice, preserved because Mercury's rotation axis is almost upright. When its propellant ran out, the spacecraft struck the surface on 30 April 2015.

image.credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Carnegie Institution of Washington
image.caption: Mercury in true colour and in enhanced colour, from MESSENGER images.

title: New Horizons
subtitle: NASA · Pluto and Kuiper Belt flyby, 2006–present

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (mission managed by Johns Hopkins APL)

facts.label: Status (October 2026)
facts.value: Extended mission in the Kuiper Belt, focused on heliophysics

essay:
New Horizons was the first spacecraft to explore Pluto and its moons up close. It was the first mission in NASA's New Frontiers programme and is powered by a radioisotope generator that was a spare from the Cassini mission.

An Atlas V and a solid-fuel upper stage sent it away from Earth on 19 January 2006 at about 58,500 km/h, the highest launch speed of any human-made object relative to Earth. A gravity assist from Jupiter on 28 February 2007 added about 14,000 km/h and cut three years off the journey. After more than nine years in flight it passed 12,500 km from Pluto on 14 July 2015. On the way it had also photographed Jupiter's moons Io, Europa and Ganymede during the 2007 flyby.

On 1 January 2019 it flew past Arrokoth, a small Kuiper Belt object that is the most distant body ever explored at close range. By October 2024 it was 60 times as far from the Sun as Earth is. NASA has extended the mission in a low-activity mode that focuses on heliophysics, measuring the outer heliosphere while preserving fuel in case a reachable flyby target is found, with operations planned until the spacecraft leaves the Kuiper Belt in 2028 or 2029.

image.credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Southwest Research Institute
image.caption: Enhanced-colour view of Pluto taken by New Horizons on 14 July 2015.

sources.title: NASA: New Horizons to Continue Exploring Outer Solar System

title: Dawn
subtitle: NASA · Vesta and Ceres orbiter, 2007–2018
essay:
Dawn spent long periods in orbit around two very different worlds: Vesta, a giant asteroid, and Ceres, a dwarf planet. Both lie in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. The mission's aim was to compare two very different survivors from the early solar system and learn about the conditions in which planets formed.

To reach both, Dawn used solar-electric ion propulsion: three thrusters, based on those of Deep Space 1, that accelerated ionized xenon. Its two solar wings spanned 19.7 m tip to tip. After a Mars gravity assist in February 2009 it reached Vesta on 16 July 2011 and spent more than a year mapping it from successively lower orbits.

Dawn left Vesta on 5 September 2012 and entered orbit around Ceres on 6 March 2015, eventually descending to a circular orbit just 375 km above the surface. The spacecraft's cameras, a visible and infrared mapping spectrometer and a gamma-ray and neutron detector measured the shape, composition and gravity of both worlds. Communications ended on 31 October 2018. Dawn remains in an orbit around Ceres that is expected to be stable for several hundred years.

image.caption: Asteroid Vesta photographed by Dawn's framing camera on 24 July 2011.

title: Kepler
subtitle: NASA · Exoplanet survey telescope, 2009–2018

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (principal investigator at Ames Research Center)

facts.label: Field of view
facts.value: About 150,000 stars in Cygnus and Lyra, monitored continuously

essay:
Kepler was NASA's first mission dedicated to finding planets around other stars. It stared at a single patch of sky in Cygnus and Lyra, watching about 150,000 stars at once for the tiny, regular dips in brightness that occur when a planet passes in front of its star. To keep that field steadily in view it orbited the Sun rather than the Earth, trailing behind our planet. Its telescope had a 1.4 m mirror and fed what was then the largest digital camera launched into space.

Within six weeks it found its first five planets, and in 2010 it found Kepler-9, the first confirmed system with more than one planet transiting the same star. In May 2013 the second of its four reaction wheels failed, ending the original mission. Engineers then used the pressure of sunlight to help stabilize the spacecraft, and the extended K2 mission surveyed fields along the ecliptic instead. It completed 19 campaigns and raised the number of stars Kepler surveyed to more than 500,000.

NASA retired Kepler on 30 October 2018 when it ran out of fuel. It discovered more than 2,600 planets and showed that the most common planet size in the galaxy is between those of Earth and Neptune, a size that does not occur in our solar system. Analysis of its data suggests that 20 to 50 percent of stars visible in the night sky may have small, possibly rocky planets in their habitable zones.

image.caption: Artist's concept of the Kepler spacecraft.

title: Juno
subtitle: NASA · Jupiter polar orbiter, 2016–present

facts.label: Jupiter orbit insertion
facts.value: 5 July 2016, 03:53 UTC (4 July in US time zones)

facts.label: Power
facts.value: Solar arrays, about 400 W at Jupiter

facts.label: Status (October 2026)
facts.value: Listed by NASA as an active mission; extended mission funded to September 2025

essay:
Juno is the first solar-powered spacecraft to operate at Jupiter and the first mission to orbit an outer planet from pole to pole. It was launched on 5 August 2011, used an Earth flyby in October 2013 to gain speed, and entered orbit around Jupiter on 5 July 2016 (4 July in the United States). Jupiter receives only about 4 percent as much sunlight as Earth, so Juno carries three large solar wings, and its electronics sit inside a titanium vault that shields them from Jupiter's intense radiation.

Its long, looping orbits take it low over the cloud tops on each close pass. Juno found that the coloured bands of Jupiter's atmosphere extend about 3,000 km down into the planet, that the core is much larger than expected yet partly dissolved, and that the magnetic field is larger and more powerful than predicted. It also found previously unseen networks of large storms swirling around the poles.

After completing its primary mission by mid-2021, Juno began an extended mission that added close flybys of three Galilean moons: Ganymede in June 2021, Europa in September 2022, where its data helped measure the thickness of the ice shell, and Io in December 2023 and February 2024. That extension was scheduled to run to September 2025. NASA's mission page still lists Juno as an active mission; when operations end, the spacecraft's orbit will decay and it will burn up in Jupiter's atmosphere.

image.caption: Artist's concept of the Juno spacecraft at Jupiter.

title: Curiosity
subtitle: NASA · Mars Science Laboratory rover, 2012–present

facts.label: Power
facts.value: Radioisotope thermoelectric generator, 125 W at start of mission

facts.label: Status (October 2026)
facts.value: Operating; reached 1 km of elevation gain on Mount Sharp on 26 August 2026

essay:
Curiosity is the rover of NASA's Mars Science Laboratory mission. When it launched in November 2011 it was the largest and most capable rover sent to Mars: about the size of a small SUV, with a mass of 899 kg, a 2.2 m robotic arm, 17 cameras and 10 science instruments, including a laser that vaporizes pinpoint spots on rocks to read their chemistry. It is powered by a radioisotope generator rather than solar panels.

It landed in Gale Crater on 6 August 2012. The mission's central question is whether Mars ever had conditions able to support microbial life, and early in the mission its instruments found chemical and mineral evidence of past habitable environments in the rocks of Gale Crater. Curiosity drills into rock and delivers the powder to onboard laboratories; it has collected 42 drilled samples. In a mudstone sample called Cumberland it found decane, undecane and dodecane, the largest organic molecules yet detected on Mars, which researchers have suggested may be fragments of fatty acids.

The rover has since been climbing Mount Sharp, the mountain in the centre of Gale Crater, reading the layered rock record as it goes. On 26 August 2026 it reached an elevation gain of 1 km above its starting point. It remains in operation more than 14 years after landing.

image.caption: Self-portrait of Curiosity on Vera Rubin Ridge, with Mount Sharp behind it.

sources.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: Mars Science Laboratory

title: Rosetta
subtitle: ESA · Comet orbiter and lander, 2004–2016

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: ESA, with contributions from member states and NASA

facts.label: End of mission
facts.value: 30 September 2016, controlled descent onto the comet

essay:
Rosetta was the first mission to rendezvous with a comet, the first to follow one along its orbit around the Sun, and the first to put a lander on a comet's surface. Its target was comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko. ESA led the mission, with contributions from its member states and NASA; the Philae lander was built by a consortium led by DLR, MPS, CNES and ASI.

Launched on an Ariane 5 in March 2004, Rosetta needed three Earth flybys and one Mars flyby to match the comet's orbit, and passed the asteroids Šteins and Lutetia on the way. To save power far from the Sun it spent 31 months in hibernation, from June 2011 to January 2014. It reached the comet on 6 August 2014 and released Philae on 12 November 2014.

Rosetta stayed with 67P through its closest approach to the Sun in August 2015, watching how solar heating changed the nucleus and its coma. It showed how the comet got its double-lobed shape, found molecular oxygen and nitrogen, and measured water with a different composition from the water in Earth's oceans. It also detected the amino acid glycine and phosphorus, both important ingredients for life. The mission ended on 30 September 2016, when the spacecraft was guided down onto the comet's surface.

image.caption: Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko in a four-image mosaic from Rosetta's navigation camera, taken 28 km from the comet on 31 January 2015.

title: Gaia
subtitle: ESA · Astrometry observatory at L2, 2013–2025

facts.label: Orbit
facts.value: Lissajous-type orbit around the Sun–Earth L2 point

facts.label: Observations made
facts.value: More than three trillion, of about two billion objects

facts.label: Status (October 2026)
facts.value: Retired; data releases continue (DR4 expected December 2026)

essay:
Gaia was an ESA observatory built to measure the positions, distances and motions of stars with very high precision. From 27 July 2014 to 15 January 2025 it made more than three trillion observations of about two billion stars and other objects, roughly 1 percent of the stars in the Milky Way. For more than 99.9 percent of those objects, no accurate distance had been measured before.

The spacecraft worked from an orbit around the Sun–Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million km from Earth. It spun slowly, sweeping two telescopes across the whole sky, and focused their light onto a single camera of nearly a billion pixels, the largest flown in space. Repeated measurements of the same stars over years revealed their tiny yearly shifts in position, from which distances follow, and their motions across the sky.

Gaia's data are released in stages; the latest full release came in June 2022. The results showed that the Milky Way merged with another large galaxy about 10 billion years ago, that the thick disc began forming 13 billion years ago, and that cooling white dwarfs turn solid. Gaia also improved the orbits of near-Earth asteroids and found new stellar streams, clusters and hypervelocity stars. Observations ended in January 2025. A fourth data release is expected in December 2026 and a final one not before the end of 2030.

image.credit: ESA/Gaia/DPAC; CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO. Acknowledgement: A. Moitinho.
image.caption: The whole sky in the brightness and colour of more than 1.8 billion stars measured by Gaia, from Early Data Release 3.

title: OSIRIS-REx
subtitle: NASA · Asteroid sample return, 2016–2023; continuing as OSIRIS-APEX

facts.label: Status (October 2026)
facts.value: Spacecraft operating as OSIRIS-APEX, bound for asteroid Apophis (arrival June 2029)

essay:
OSIRIS-REx was the first US mission to collect a sample from an asteroid. Its target was Bennu, a carbonaceous near-Earth asteroid. Scientists hope the sample will show whether asteroids that struck the young Earth delivered water and other ingredients for life.

Launched in September 2016, the spacecraft reached Bennu on 3 December 2018 and entered orbit on 31 December, the smallest body ever orbited by a spacecraft. Close-up mapping showed a surface far rockier than expected, covered in boulders, which made finding a safe sampling spot difficult. The team chose a site called Nightingale inside a 140 m crater. On 20 October 2020 the spacecraft briefly touched the surface in a touch-and-go manoeuvre, firing a burst of nitrogen gas to stir loose rock and dust into its sampler head.

OSIRIS-REx left Bennu in May 2021 and on 24 September 2023 released a capsule that parachuted onto the Utah Test and Training Range. It held 121.6 g of asteroid material, more than double the mission's requirement and the largest asteroid sample collected in space. The spacecraft itself was renamed OSIRIS-APEX and redirected to the asteroid Apophis. After an Earth flyby on 23 September 2025, it is due to arrive in June 2029, shortly after Apophis passes within about 32,000 km of Earth's surface.

image.caption: An Atlas V rocket lifting off from Cape Canaveral with OSIRIS-REx on 8 September 2016.

title: Parker Solar Probe
subtitle: NASA · Solar orbiter, 2018–present

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (Goddard Space Flight Center and Johns Hopkins APL)

facts.label: Launch vehicle
facts.value: Delta IV Heavy with upper stage, Cape Canaveral

facts.label: Closest approach to the Sun
facts.value: About 6.2 million km from the surface

essay:
Parker Solar Probe is the first spacecraft to fly through the Sun's corona, its outer atmosphere. NASA announced on 14 December 2021 that it had passed through the corona and sampled the particles and magnetic fields there. The mission is named for Eugene Parker, who proposed the existence of the solar wind in 1958; it was the first NASA spacecraft named after a living person.

After launch on a Delta IV Heavy in August 2018, Parker used seven flybys of Venus, the last on 6 November 2024, to shrink its orbit step by step. Its closest passes, beginning on 24 December 2024, bring it within about 6.2 million km of the solar surface, at about 700,000 km/h.

The spacecraft survives behind an 11.43 cm carbon-composite heat shield that can withstand nearly 1,377 °C, while its solar arrays are actively cooled. Its four instrument suites measure electric and magnetic fields, energetic particles and the solar wind, and image the corona. The aim is to answer long-standing questions: why the corona is far hotter than the visible surface, how the solar wind is accelerated, and where high-energy solar particles come from. These measurements also help forecast space weather at Earth.

image.caption: A Delta IV Heavy rocket launching Parker Solar Probe from Cape Canaveral on 12 August 2018.

sources.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: Parker Solar Probe

title: TESS
subtitle: NASA · Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, 2018–present

facts.label: Survey targets
facts.value: About 200,000 of the brightest stars near the Sun

essay:
The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, TESS, searches for planets around nearby bright stars. It looks for transits: the small, repeated dips in a star's brightness that occur when a planet passes in front of it.

TESS was launched on a Falcon 9 on 18 April 2018. Its main survey targets are about 200,000 of the brightest stars near the Sun. Planets found around such nearby, bright stars give astronomers a rich set of targets for more detailed follow-up studies with other telescopes. Before launch the team expected thousands of planet candidates, around 300 of them no more than twice the size of Earth.

TESS completed its two-year primary mission and has since continued in extended missions. By September 2025, at the end of its second extended mission, it had identified nearly 6,000 confirmed or candidate exoplanets. Its repeated wide-field images are also used to study many other objects that change in brightness, from nearby asteroids to pulsating stars and distant galaxies containing supernovae.

image.caption: A Falcon 9 rocket lifting off from Cape Canaveral with TESS on 18 April 2018.

title: Perseverance
subtitle: NASA · Mars 2020 rover, 2021–present

facts.label: Ingenuity first flight
facts.value: 19 April 2021 (first powered flight on another planet)

facts.label: Distance driven
facts.value: 45.22 km by 11 October 2026, the off-world record

essay:
Perseverance is the rover of NASA's Mars 2020 mission. Its job is to look for signs of ancient microbial life and to collect cores of Martian rock and regolith that a future mission could bring back to Earth. It is based on the Curiosity design, with a mass of about 1,050 kg and a radioisotope power source.

The rover landed on 18 February 2021 in Jezero Crater, on the western edge of the Isidis Planitia basin. It carried a small helicopter, Ingenuity, which made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet on 19 April 2021, hovering for 30 seconds at 3 m. A separate experiment, MOXIE, demonstrated making oxygen from the carbon dioxide atmosphere. In its first five years the rover collected more than two dozen geologically diverse rock samples and explored the history of water and habitable environments in the crater and on its rim.

In 2024 Perseverance sampled a rock nicknamed Cheyava Falls. After a year of peer review, a study published in Nature in September 2025 reported that the sample contains potential biosignatures: features that could have a biological origin but need more study before any conclusion can be drawn. On 11 October 2026 the rover's odometer reached 45.22 km, passing Opportunity's record for the longest distance driven on another world.

image.caption: Perseverance's selfie with the Ingenuity helicopter, about 3.9 m away, on 6 April 2021.

title: Lucy
subtitle: NASA · Trojan asteroid flybys, 2021–present

facts.label: Main-belt flybys
facts.value: Dinkinesh and Selam (1 November 2023); Donaldjohanson (20 April 2025)

facts.label: Trojan flybys planned
facts.value: Eurybates and Queta (11 August 2027) through Patroclus and Menoetius (3 March 2033)

facts.label: Status (October 2026)
facts.value: Operating, cruising toward the first Trojan flyby

essay:
Lucy is the first mission to explore the Jupiter Trojans, two swarms of asteroids that share Jupiter's orbit around the Sun, one leading the planet by 60° and one trailing it. The Trojans are thought to be remnants of the same material that formed the outer planets, preserved since the early solar system.

The spacecraft is more than 16 m from tip to tip, mostly because of its two circular solar arrays, each over 7 m across. It carries a high-resolution camera, a colour imager and infrared spectrometer, and a thermal infrared spectrometer. Lucy launched on 16 October 2021 and returned to Earth for gravity assists before heading out. On 1 November 2023 it passed the small main-belt asteroid Dinkinesh and found that it has a moon, now named Selam, which is itself a contact binary. On 20 April 2025 it flew past a second main-belt asteroid, Donaldjohanson.

Lucy's tour is planned to cover 11 asteroids in total, a record for a single mission. The first Trojan encounter, with Eurybates and its satellite Queta, is scheduled for 11 August 2027, followed by Polymele in September 2027, Leucus in 2028 and Orus in 2028. The tour ends with the binary pair Patroclus and Menoetius on 3 March 2033.

image.caption: An Atlas V rocket launching Lucy from Cape Canaveral before dawn on 16 October 2021.

title: James Webb Space Telescope
subtitle: NASA, ESA and CSA · Infrared space observatory at L2, 2021–present

facts.label: Primary mirror
facts.value: 18 gold-coated beryllium segments, 6.6 m across flat to flat

essay:
The James Webb Space Telescope is a large infrared observatory built by NASA with the European and Canadian space agencies. It studies every phase of cosmic history, from the first galaxies that formed after the Big Bang to the formation of stars and planetary systems and the planets of our own solar system.

Webb's primary mirror is made of 18 hexagonal segments of gold-coated beryllium that together span 6.6 m, with a collecting area of 25 square metres. The mirror and the five-layer sunshield, roughly 10 by 22 m, were folded to fit inside an Ariane 5 rocket and unfolded in space. To see faint infrared light the telescope must be very cold, so the sunshield keeps it permanently shaded from the Sun, Earth and Moon. Four main instruments cover wavelengths from 0.6 to 29 micrometres.

Webb launched from Kourou on 25 December 2021. Unlike Hubble it does not orbit Earth: on 24 January 2022 it reached an orbit around the second Sun–Earth Lagrange point, L2, about 1.5 million km from Earth. Commissioning was completed and the observatory is operating normally; its station-keeping propellant is expected to last about 10 years. It is designed to look back more than 13.5 billion years to some of the first galaxies to form after the Big Bang.

image.caption: Ariane 5 rocket launching the James Webb Space Telescope from Kourou, French Guiana, on 25 December 2021.

sources.title: NASA Science: James Webb Space Telescope
NSSDCA Master Catalog: James Webb Space Telescope

title: DART
subtitle: NASA · Double Asteroid Redirection Test, 2021–2022

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (built and operated by Johns Hopkins APL)

facts.label: Target
facts.value: Dimorphos (about 160 m), moon of the asteroid Didymos (about 780 m)

facts.label: Result
facts.value: Orbit of Dimorphos shortened by 32 minutes, from 11 h 55 min to 11 h 23 min

essay:
DART, the Double Asteroid Redirection Test, was the first mission to test a method of planetary defence: changing an asteroid's motion by deliberately crashing a spacecraft into it. Its target was Dimorphos, a moonlet about 160 m across that orbits a larger asteroid, Didymos, about 780 m across. Neither poses any threat to Earth. Because Dimorphos orbits Didymos, any change in its speed shows up as a change in its orbital period, which telescopes on Earth can measure.

DART launched on a Falcon 9 from Vandenberg in November 2021. It carried one instrument, the DRACO camera, which fed images to an autonomous navigation system that steered the spacecraft onto Dimorphos during the last hours. Fifteen days before impact the Italian Space Agency's LICIACube cubesat separated to follow about three minutes behind and photograph the collision. On 26 September 2022 DART hit Dimorphos at about 6.6 km/s, about 11 million km from Earth, sending back images until about two seconds before impact.

NASA had set a minimum target of shortening the orbit by 73 seconds. Measurements showed that the impact cut the orbital period by 32 minutes, from 11 hours 55 minutes to 11 hours 23 minutes. That was more than 25 times the minimum. ESA's Hera mission is planned to visit the system to study the result in more detail.

image.caption: Illustration of DART approaching the Didymos system before impact on Dimorphos.

sources.title: NASA: NASA Confirms DART Mission Impact Changed Asteroid's Motion in Space

title: Artemis I
subtitle: NASA · Uncrewed lunar flight test, 2022

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, with ESA providing Orion's service module

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 16 November 2022, 06:47 UTC, Launch Complex 39B, Kennedy Space Center

facts.label: Splashdown
facts.value: 11 December 2022, Pacific Ocean off San Diego

essay:
Artemis I was the first integrated flight test of NASA's new deep-space system: the Space Launch System rocket, the Orion spacecraft and the ground systems at Kennedy Space Center. It flew without a crew to prove the hardware before astronauts used it.

The SLS lifted off from Launch Complex 39B at 1:47 a.m. EST on 16 November 2022. Its upper stage sent Orion toward the Moon and released ten small cubesats on separate missions. Orion flew close past the Moon, then entered a wide orbit that took it 70,000 km (43,471 miles) beyond the lunar far side. At its farthest it was 432,210 km from Earth. It then returned and splashed down in the Pacific off San Diego on 11 December 2022, after 25 days, 10 hours and 53 minutes.

The SLS met or exceeded its performance targets, and Orion completed 161 test objectives, including 20 added during the flight. The European-built service module produced about 20 percent more power than expected. Engineers found more charring than predicted on Orion's heat shield, and the analysis fed into changes for later missions. The success of Artemis I led to Artemis II, which carried four astronauts around the Moon in 2026.

image.caption: Orion, with Earth and the Moon in view, on flight day 13 of Artemis I, when it reached its maximum distance from Earth.

title: Europa Clipper
subtitle: NASA · Jupiter orbiter for Europa flybys, 2024–present

facts.label: Launch vehicle
facts.value: Falcon Heavy, Launch Complex 39A, Kennedy Space Center

facts.label: Size
facts.value: More than 30 m across with solar arrays deployed

essay:
Europa Clipper is the first mission designed to study Jupiter's moon Europa in detail. Its main goal is to find out whether there are places beneath Europa's icy surface that could support life. Scientists think a salty ocean lies under the ice that may hold more than twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans combined.

The spacecraft is solar-powered. With its arrays deployed it spans more than 30 m, about the length of a basketball court. Its main body consists of an avionics vault, a radio frequency module and a propulsion module, and it has a 3 m high-gain antenna. It carries nine science instruments plus a gravity experiment that uses its radio system, and all the instruments will operate together on every pass.

Europa Clipper launched on a Falcon Heavy on 14 October 2024. It flew past Mars in 2025 and is due to swing past Earth on 3 December 2026 for a final gravity assist before arriving at Jupiter in April 2030, after a journey of about 2.9 billion km. It will not orbit Europa itself. Instead it will orbit Jupiter and make 49 close flybys of the moon, using an orbital tour design derived from the way Cassini explored Saturn's moons.

image.caption: Artist's concept of Europa Clipper approaching Jupiter and Europa.

title: JUICE
subtitle: ESA · Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer, 2023–present

facts.label: Gravity assists
facts.value: Moon and Earth (August 2024), Venus (August 2025), Earth (28 September 2026), Earth (January 2029)

essay:
JUICE, the Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer, is ESA's mission to Jupiter and three of its large moons: Ganymede, Callisto and Europa. All three are thought to have oceans beneath their ice. The mission will study them both as worlds in their own right and as possible habitats, explore Jupiter's environment, and treat the Jupiter system as a model for gas giants around other stars. NASA is collaborating on the ESA-led mission.

Juice launched on an Ariane 5 from French Guiana on 14 April 2023. Its route uses a series of gravity assists. In August 2024 it made a combined lunar-Earth flyby, and in August 2025 it flew past Venus. On 28 September 2026 it passed 8,640 km above the Indian Ocean, and its JANUS camera, one of 10 instruments on board, photographed a long strip of southern Africa as Earth turned below. A final Earth flyby in January 2029 will send it on to Jupiter.

Juice is due to arrive in July 2031. It carries solar wings with a total area of 85 square metres to generate power so far from the Sun. The plan includes 35 close flybys of Jupiter's moons, with the aim of characterizing Ganymede, Callisto and Europa as planetary objects and as possible habitats.

image.caption: A strip of southern Africa from Madagascar to the Gulf of Guinea, imaged by Juice's JANUS camera during its Earth flyby on 28 September 2026.

sources.title: ESA: Fly over Africa with Juice

title: Psyche
subtitle: NASA · Metal asteroid orbiter, 2023–present

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (Discovery programme; spacecraft operations by JPL)

facts.label: Launch vehicle
facts.value: Falcon Heavy, Launch Complex 39A, Kennedy Space Center

facts.label: Propulsion
facts.value: Solar-electric, four SPT-140 Hall-effect thrusters using xenon

facts.label: Status (October 2026)
facts.value: In cruise to the asteroid belt

essay:
Psyche is a NASA mission to the asteroid of the same name, a body in the main asteroid belt whose surface appears to contain a large amount of metal rather than rock or ice. Scientists think it may be part of the metal core of a planetesimal, one of the building blocks of the early planets. Psyche is the first mission to explore such a world, and its results should improve our knowledge of iron cores, a previously unexplored building block of planet formation.

The spacecraft is box-shaped and, with its solar arrays deployed, almost as large as a tennis court. Its arrays drive a solar-electric propulsion system of Hall-effect thrusters that use xenon propellant. It carries a multispectral imager, a gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer and a magnetometer, and will measure the asteroid's gravity through its radio signal. It also carries the Deep Space Optical Communications experiment, NASA's test of laser communication beyond the Moon.

Psyche launched on a Falcon Heavy on 13 October 2023. On 15 May 2026 it flew past Mars, using the planet's gravity to gain speed and tilt its trajectory, and photographed Mars to calibrate its instruments for the work ahead. It is due to reach the asteroid in August 2029 and will spend about two years in a series of orbits, mapping the surface and measuring its composition, gravity and magnetic field to test whether Psyche is an exposed core.

image.caption: Illustration of the Psyche spacecraft.
